title: Closed-loop monomers from real mixed plastic waste

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an integrated process that continuously turns real mixed plastic packaging into polymer-grade ethylene and propylene, the small molecules used to manufacture polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP). Its intended feed contains these plastics alongside specified, representative amounts of PVC, PET, fillers and food residue. Success would require selective chemistry, reliable reactor operation and purification that together deliver competitively priced monomers with lower life-cycle emissions than defined virgin fossil alternatives, without depending on a large virgin-olefin co-feed. This is the target capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement.

Here, closed-loop refers to recovering useful monomer feedstocks for new plastics. Converting PE carbon into a mixture of ethylene and propylene would create feedstock circularity, even though it would not recover only the original monomer of each input polymer. Likewise, accepting contaminated packaging does not mean converting every constituent into light olefins. A credible process must account explicitly for contaminants, pretreatment, rejected material and by-products.

significance.text: The potential resource base is large. Plastics Europe's Fast Facts 2025 gives rounded, preliminary estimates of 430.9 million tonnes of global plastics production in 2024, with 89.8% fossil-based. Within the report's defined production scope, low- and linear-low-density PE account for 13.9%, high- and medium-density PE for 12.1%, and PP for 19.0%: together, 45.0%. These are production shares, distinct from the statement in Bi and colleagues' paper that polyolefins account for more than half of plastic waste.

If achieved, economical recovery of polymer-grade monomers from difficult packaging waste would expand the supply of circular chemical feedstocks, including from streams unsuitable for mechanical recycling. The immediate consequence would be usable monomer output from the demonstrated feed. Substantial displacement of virgin production would additionally require widespread deployment, adequate collection, sustained catalyst performance and economical purification. A plant producing tonnes per day could establish an important engineering capability without establishing globally consequential supply.

As an interpretive analogy, its ambition resembles breakthroughs that made essential materials, such as steel, economical at much greater scale. The analogy concerns cost and material availability; it does not predict equivalent historical impact or establish that recycling can expand without collection and infrastructure constraints. Collection, sorting policy and product design would remain necessary complements. CHE-07 targets a substantial packaging and polyolefin opportunity, rather than complete recovery of every atom of every chemical.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central chemical barrier is selectivity: direct cracking of polyolefins produces a broad mixture because competing bond-breaking and secondary reactions divert material away from ethylene and propylene. The needed advance is to preserve high recovery of the desired light olefins while processing variable waste feeds, then separate and purify those products efficiently. A high reactor yield alone does not establish a viable source of polymer-grade monomers.

Contaminant tolerance remains a concrete obstacle. Bi and colleagues tested selected waste polyolefins, but the supplied review does not identify a demonstration using unsorted packaging containing the full PVC, PET, filler and food-residue mixture envisaged here. Their supplementary experiments found that strongly basic nitrogen-containing additives substantially inhibited catalytic activity and discussed possible pretreatment. This establishes a specific sensitivity, without establishing that all contaminants behave similarly or that every contaminated stream is unusable.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining integrated challenge includes sustained feeding and conversion of heterogeneous material, catalyst lifetime and regeneration, management of contaminants and residues, and product separation at useful throughput. Pretreatment may be part of a successful system, but its inputs, costs and rejected fractions must be included when assessing waste tolerance. The supplied economic and emissions analysis excludes subsequent product separation, leaving a material gap between promising reaction chemistry and competitive delivered monomers.

The supplied record establishes progress toward this target, rather than a worldwide inventory of remaining capabilities as of 1 November 2026. Its freshness record contains no current search coverage. The complete capability therefore remains unestablished in these inputs, while its absence everywhere at that date is also unestablished.

current_state.text: On 14 October 2025, Bi, Chen, Lin and colleagues reported a tandem zeolite process converting PE into ethylene and propylene at up to 79% carbon molar yield, without noble metals, external hydrogen or added olefins. This is a published laboratory result. The yield uses the paper's stated carbon-molar normalization; it is not a measure of shipped polymer-grade product. The authors place conventional catalytic cracking below 25% yield of these olefins, while also discussing pulsed-heating results of 36–45%, so the conventional-cracking comparison should not be read as a ceiling for all earlier approaches.

Optimized experiments used 100 mg of PE, with a first-stage temperature program from 260 to 300°C and a second stage at 540°C. The continuous experiment lasted eight hours, but the Methods specify 600 mg of PE dosed over six hours at approximately 100 mg per hour. Thus, an eight-hour run and six-hour feeding period reconcile the reported descriptions; eight hours of uninterrupted feeding is not established. These experiments demonstrate laboratory operation, far below the proposed tonnes-per-day scale.

The study also tested selected waste HDPE, LDPE and PP powders. These broaden the evidence beyond clean laboratory PE, but do not establish tolerance of unsorted multilayer packaging with representative PVC, PET and food residues. The observed inhibition by strongly basic nitrogen-containing additives further limits generalization to arbitrary waste feeds. Eliminating an external olefin feed is a relevant advance for PE conversion; broad mixed-waste performance remains a separate question.

The paper's preliminary economics and emissions comparisons use a PE-pyrolysis route as the comparator. The supplementary analysis excludes subsequent product separation costs and emissions. These modeled comparisons therefore do not establish the delivered cost of polymer-grade monomers or life-cycle superiority to virgin fossil monomer production. Those conclusions require an integrated boundary covering purification and an explicit virgin-production benchmark.

The earlier research notes attribute to Conk, Stahler, Shi, Bell, Hartwig and colleagues a Science report dated 29 August 2024 using tungsten oxide on silica and sodium on alumina at 320°C, with greater than 90% yield from PE, PP or mixtures, including postconsumer forms, to propylene or propylene plus isobutylene. However, no Conk source artifact was retained for the supplied review. Those catalyst, temperature, yield and feed-scope details remain unverified here, rather than disproved. Bi and colleagues provide narrower secondary evidence that earlier Conk routes reacted PE or PP with excess ethylene, discussing earlier ethylene-assisted routes at 15–20 bar. A high reported product yield from such a route cannot by itself establish recovery of waste-derived carbon without a virgin co-feed.

Plastics Europe estimates chemically recycled production at 0.37 million tonnes for 2024, compared with 430.9 million tonnes of total plastics production. Its estimate uses fuel-use-exempt mass-balance attribution and includes secondary chemicals usable for plastics or other materials. It illustrates the small reported scale of this attributed category, but does not directly measure selective waste-to-monomer plants or actual monomer output. The original notes also asserted commercial availability of pyrolysis and PET methanolysis; the supplied reviewed evidence does not verify those deployment claims or establish PET methanolysis's comparative maturity.

The supplied review assessed complete, untruncated text extractions of Bi and colleagues' article and supplement and the Plastics Europe report. Although the article's resolved web address contained a cookie-error parameter, its retained HTML contained the complete article text. Figures and graphical details were not visually inspected; the quantitative account above relies on the reviewed text, Methods, captions and extracted chart labels. The Conk article has no retained artifact, so the original notes' description of abstract-only access does not provide an independently verified abstract in this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a continuous plant on characterized real post-consumer mixed packaging containing PE, PP and specified representative concentrations of PVC, PET, fillers and food residue, and ship tonnes per day of polymer-grade ethylene and propylene. Publish the feed composition, product specifications, throughput and operating duration. Tonnes per day is a proposed milestone for this concept, not an established consensus standard. A high-yield batch experiment on clean PE would demonstrate a narrower capability.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting requirements: publish complete mass and carbon balances across pretreatment, reaction, purification, internal recycle, rejected material and by-products. Identify the origin and fate of any external carbon feed so that added virgin olefin cannot be mistaken for recovered waste carbon. Demonstrate operation without dependence on a stoichiometric virgin-ethylene feed, and report catalyst consumption, activity loss, regeneration and replacement over a duration adequate to assess sustained performance.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed accounting requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical acceptance criteria: establish delivered monomer cost and life-cycle emissions below explicitly defined virgin fossil benchmarks, including feed preparation, utilities, catalyst use, separation, purification and residue management. This boundary addresses the separation omissions in the supplied laboratory study. Its favorable preliminary comparison with PE pyrolysis would not alone satisfy the proposed virgin-monomer comparison.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical acceptance criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope tests: repeat the demonstration across independently characterized waste lots, disclose operating conditions and analytical methods, and obtain independent verification or replication of yield, purity and balances. Establish feed-acceptance limits and show how performance changes near those limits, including contaminant-sensitive conditions. Such tests would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested feed envelope; finite experiments cannot establish tolerance of every packaging composition or literal universal recyclability.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and scope tests

related_concepts.text: Conceptual relationship to CHE-03, Fossil-parity olefins and liquid fuels from carbon dioxide: both seek competitive alternatives to fossil-derived chemical feedstocks, and their olefin products could overlap. CHE-03 begins with CO2; CHE-07 begins with carbon already incorporated into waste plastics. Their feed preparation, reaction chemistry and energy requirements remain distinct.

Conceptual relationship to CHE-04, Plant-scale molecular separations that can retire the hardest distillations, and CHE-05, First-time-right scale-up of multiphase reactors: CHE-07 needs economical product purification and reliable scale-up from small experiments to sustained heterogeneous-feed operation. Advances in either area could support it. Neither entry alone establishes selective conversion or tolerance of contaminated packaging, and CHE-07 does not require that every successful separation retire a distillation.

Conceptual relationship to CHE-06, Direct solar manufacture of fuels and chemicals: both could contribute to lower-emissions chemical supply, but CHE-07 does not specify direct solar energy conversion. CHE-09, Direct air capture near the thermodynamic limit, at climate scale, also concerns carbon management, while addressing atmospheric CO2 capture rather than recovery of existing plastic carbon.

Conceptual relationship to CHE-10, On-demand manufacturing of arbitrary small molecules: ethylene and propylene are small molecules, but CHE-07 targets a limited set of bulk products from variable waste. Producing those products selectively does not demonstrate arbitrary molecular synthesis, and arbitrary synthesis would not by itself establish mixed-waste recycling economics.

The remaining roster entries—CHE-01, Ambient nitrogen fixation at industrial rate, efficiency, and lifetime; CHE-02, High-yield direct oxidation of methane to methanol with dioxygen; and CHE-08, Land-free staple calories from carbon dioxide and renewable energy—share broad concerns with selective chemistry, efficiency or industrial operation. Their reactants, products and practical goals differ substantially, so these common engineering themes do not make them the same innovation.

Beyond the roster, mechanical recycling, pyrolysis-based feedstock recovery and PET methanolysis are relevant neighboring approaches. CHE-07 seeks selective monomer recovery from difficult polyolefin-rich packaging, rather than physical reprocessing or broad cracking-product recovery. PET methanolysis addresses a distinct polymer chemistry; its success would not establish the proposed PE/PP capability. Comparative commercial maturity and deployment of these approaches are not resolved by the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Preserved CHE-07's identity while defining closed-loop operation as feedstock circularity and separating contaminant acceptance from conversion of every constituent into olefins.
change_log.reason: Recovery of PE carbon as ethylene plus propylene is useful circularity without exact original-monomer recovery or universal constituent conversion.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical weak-bond explanation with the documented problem of competing cracking and secondary reactions.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence directly supports poor selectivity but does not independently establish the original weak-bond formulation.

change_log.change: Qualified claims of worldwide absence, commercial pyrolysis deployment and comparative PET-methanolysis maturity.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources and empty freshness record do not establish those claims as of 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Specified the 79% result as carbon molar yield, retained laboratory temperatures and scale, and corrected the continuous experiment to an eight-hour run with six hours of feeding.
change_log.reason: These distinctions preserve the measured achievement while reconciling the narrative with the Methods.

change_log.change: Added selected waste-polyolefin tests, nitrogen-additive inhibition and the 36–45% pulsed-heating comparison.
change_log.reason: These details define demonstrated feed breadth and prevent overgeneralization of both contaminant tolerance and the below-25% conventional-cracking comparison.

change_log.change: Retained the original Conk quantitative claims as explicitly unverified attributions and used Bi's account for the narrower excess-ethylene finding.
change_log.reason: The missing primary artifact limits verification without proving the reported results false.

change_log.change: Distinguished preliminary economics and emissions modeling from integrated polymer-grade monomer performance.
change_log.reason: The reviewed analysis excludes subsequent separation and compares against PE pyrolysis rather than establishing superiority to virgin fossil production.

change_log.change: Preserved production statistics while adding preliminary-estimate, scope and mass-balance attribution caveats.
change_log.reason: The 0.37-million-tonne category is not a direct measurement of selective monomer recovery, and production shares differ from waste shares.

change_log.change: Retained the materials-scale impact analogy as an interpretation and separated plant demonstration from global displacement.
change_log.reason: Large downstream impact depends on collection, deployment and sustained operation beyond tonnes-per-day output.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to cover operating duration, feed limits, catalyst maintenance, complete balances, purification, independent verification and benchmark boundaries.
change_log.reason: These make the target assessable while avoiding presentation of proposed thresholds as established standards or proof of universality.

change_log.change: Added explicit relationships to the supplied roster and preserved source-access and graphical-inspection limitations.
change_log.reason: The record must stand alone without merging distinct concepts or implying document inspection beyond the supplied review.

unresolved_issues: The Conk primary source is absent from the retained evidence. Its catalyst identities, 320°C condition, greater-than-90% yield, yield basis and postconsumer feed scope require verification.
The complete field's status as of 1 November 2026 remains unknown because the supplied freshness record contains no current search coverage.
Representative contaminant concentrations, acceptable pretreatment and maximum rejected fractions have not been specified for the proposed mixed-packaging capability.
Sustained catalyst lifetime, regeneration needs and performance across variable real packaging feeds remain unestablished at the proposed scale.
Integrated purification performance, polymer-grade product specifications and delivered cost and life-cycle emissions relative to defined virgin benchmarks remain unresolved.
The proposed demonstration's operating duration, benchmark assumptions and independent-replication design still need numerical definition; tonnes per day alone is insufficient.
Commercial deployment and comparative maturity of pyrolysis and PET methanolysis are not verified by the supplied reviewed evidence.
Figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review. Quantitative interpretation rests on reviewed text, Methods, captions and extracted chart labels.

The review's recommendation to avoid affirming unverified Conk details was adopted in substance, while retaining those details as explicitly unverified attributions to preserve the original quantitative research without inventing confirmation.
